lead: Therapeutic equipment acts on the body: it paces, shocks, breathes for the patient, heats, cools and breaks stones. After this unit you can explain how each machine works, draw its block diagram, work out its output in joules, volts, litres per minute or degrees, and name its main hazard.
about: Unit 5 covers machines that deliver energy to the body or take over a body function. Chapter 5.1 starts with pacemakers and defibrillators, the two ways to correct a failing heart rhythm. 5.2 adds the heart-lung machine, which stands in for heart and lungs during surgery. 5.3 and 5.4 turn to breathing: ventilator types and modes, then the humidifiers, nebulizers and inhalers that condition the gas. 5.5 to 5.8 are energy-based therapy: diathermy heating, nerve and muscle stimulation, shock-wave lithotripsy, and cryogenic cold. 5.9 closes with the protection circuit that keeps an ECG amplifier alive during a shock, and the RF ablation catheter. Every chapter gives the principle, the block diagram, the exam numbers and the safety limits.

chapters.idea: A pacemaker gives a small timed pulse to start a heartbeat when the heart's own conduction fails; a defibrillator gives one large shock to stop chaotic fibrillation so a normal rhythm can restart.
chapters.depth: Internal (implanted) and external pacemakers: leads, unipolar and bipolar pacing, fixed-rate versus demand (R-wave inhibited) modes, pacing rate in pulses per minute, pulse width 0.5–2 ms. Battery: lithium-iodine cell, about 2.8 V, capacity in Ah; life in years = capacity ÷ average current. Defibrillators: AC (mains driven, older) and DC (capacitor discharge); internal and external; monophasic and biphasic waveforms; typical external settings 200 J biphasic, up to 360 J monophasic; synchronised cardioversion versus unsynchronised defibrillation. Keep the protection circuit for 5.9.

figure.title: Pacemaker loop
figure.aria: Block diagram of an implanted pacemaker: cell, timing circuit, output stage, lead, heart, and a sense amplifier looping back to the timer.

chapters.example: A DC defibrillator charges a 32 µF capacitor to 5000 V. Find the energy stored and the charge on the capacitor. Energy E = ½CV² = 0.5 × 32×10⁻⁶ F × (5000 V)² = 0.5 × 32×10⁻⁶ × 25×10⁶ = 400 J. Charge Q = CV = 32×10⁻⁶ F × 5000 V = 0.16 C. The 400 J stored is more than the 200 J delivered to the patient, because the rest is lost in the paddles, cables and the chest wall.
chapters.trap: Mixing up energy (joules), charge (coulombs) and voltage (volts) in the ½CV² calculation; and thinking the pacemaker powers the heart's pumping — it only triggers the muscle, the contraction itself does the pumping. Also, unsynchronised defibrillation is not the same as synchronised cardioversion.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: resting and action potentials, ECG recording. Unit 2: arrhythmia monitoring.
chapters.leave: The defibrillator protection circuit and ablation catheter go to 5.9. Arrhythmia detection and Holter monitoring stay in Unit 2.

chapters.idea: The heart-lung machine replaces the heart's pumping and the lung's gas exchange, so the surgeon can stop the heart and open it.
chapters.depth: Cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB): venous cannula, venous reservoir with level alarm, roller pump (occlusive) versus centrifugal pump, membrane and bubble oxygenators, heat exchanger, arterial filter, cardioplegia line, arterial cannula. Flow 2.2–2.4 L/min per m² of body surface area, mean arterial pressure about 50–80 mmHg, priming volume, heparinisation. Safety devices: bubble detector, level sensor, low-pressure alarm, backup battery.

figure.title: Cardiopulmonary bypass loop
figure.aria: Block diagram of the bypass circuit: venous cannula, reservoir, roller pump, oxygenator, heat exchanger and arterial cannula in series.

chapters.example: A patient is 170 cm tall and weighs 60 kg. Find the body surface area and the pump flow at 2.4 L/min/m². Mosteller BSA = √(height × weight ÷ 3600) = √(170 × 60 ÷ 3600) = √2.833 = 1.68 m². Flow = 2.4 L/min/m² × 1.68 m² = 4.04 L/min. The perfusionist sets the pump near 4 L/min, and checks the mean arterial pressure stays around 60 mmHg.
chapters.trap: Saying the oxygenator only adds oxygen — it also removes carbon dioxide, which is the lung's other job. Roller pumps are occlusive and can build pressure against a blocked line, so they need a pressure limit; centrifugal pumps are non-occlusive and can run dry.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2: cardiac output, blood flow and pressure measurement.
chapters.leave: Oxygen saturation and oximetry stay in Unit 2; blood gas and pH measurement in Unit 3.

chapters.idea: A ventilator pushes a breath in and lets it out, and the variable that ends each breath — volume, pressure, time, flow or the patient — is what names the mode.
chapters.depth: Negative-pressure and positive-pressure ventilators; invasive and non-invasive. Breath phases: trigger (what starts it), limit (what caps it), cycle (what ends it). The five cycling variables the syllabi list: pressure-cycled, volume-cycled, time-cycled, flow-cycled, patient-cycled. Modes: CMV, assist-control, SIMV, pressure support, pressure control, volume control, CPAP, PEEP. Settings: tidal volume 6–8 mL/kg predicted body weight, respiratory rate, FiO₂, I:E ratio, PEEP, alarm limits.

figure.aria: Decision tree showing the five variables that can end an inspiration and the mode each one names.

chapters.example: A male patient is 175 cm tall. Find the tidal volume range at 6–8 mL/kg of predicted body weight. Predicted body weight = 50 + 0.91 × (height in cm − 152.4) = 50 + 0.91 × 22.6 = 70.6 kg. At 6 mL/kg: 70.6 × 6 = 424 mL. At 8 mL/kg: 70.6 × 8 = 565 mL. Set tidal volume between 424 mL and 565 mL, not on the actual body weight.
chapters.trap: Naming a mode by its control variable but cycling it on something else — pressure control is usually time-cycled, not pressure-cycled. Also, predicted body weight (from height) is used for tidal volume, not the scale weight.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2: spirometry, intra-alveolar and thoracic pressures, compliance.
chapters.leave: Spirometry measurement stays in Unit 2; gas humidification is 5.4.

chapters.idea: Dry medical gas injures the airway, so water is added as vapour by a humidifier, as fine droplets by a nebulizer, or as a measured drug dose by an inhaler.
chapters.depth: Humidifiers: bubble-through, pass-over, heated-wire, and heat-and-moisture exchangers (HME, artificial nose). Nebulizers: jet (pneumatic), ultrasonic, mesh; mass median aerodynamic diameter 1–5 µm for deposition in the lower airway. Inhalers: metered-dose inhaler with spacer, dry-powder inhaler. Oxygen delivery: nasal cannula, venturi mask, face mask. Absolute humidity of saturated gas at 37 °C is 44 mg/L; the isothermic saturation boundary is normally below the carina.

figure.aria: Block diagram showing dry oxygen split into a heated humidifier path and a jet nebulizer path, both joining at the airway and leading to the alveoli.

chapters.example: A patient breathes 10 L/min of completely dry oxygen. How much water must be added per hour to bring the gas to full saturation at 37 °C, where saturated gas holds 44 mg of water per litre? Water needed = 44 mg/L × 10 L/min = 440 mg/min. Per hour: 440 × 60 = 26,400 mg = 26.4 g. A heated humidifier must supply about 26 g of water every hour, which is why its chamber runs dry if nobody refills it.
chapters.trap: Treating humidifier and nebulizer as the same thing: a humidifier adds vapour and never carries a drug, a nebulizer makes droplets and can carry one. Bigger droplets do not go deeper — droplets above about 5 µm settle in the upper airway.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2: spirometry and lung volumes; 5.3 for ventilator circuits.
chapters.leave: Ventilator modes go to 5.3; oxygen saturation measurement stays in Unit 2.

chapters.idea: Diathermy heats deep tissue by passing radio-frequency current, microwaves or ultrasound through it, without cutting the skin.
chapters.depth: Short-wave diathermy at 27.12 MHz with capacitive plates or an inductive coil; microwave diathermy at 2450 MHz with a reflector applicator; ultrasonic diathermy at 0.8–1 MHz. Heating by dielectric loss and resistive loss; penetration depth falls as frequency rises. Dose in watts and minutes; contraindications: metal implants in the field, pregnancy, ischaemic or bleeding tissue. Surgical diathermy (electrosurgery) uses the same RF principle to cut and coagulate — mention it as a separate application, not as therapy.

figure.aria: Block diagram of a short-wave diathermy unit from mains to RF oscillator, amplifier, matching network, applicator plates and deep tissue.

chapters.example: A short-wave diathermy unit works at 27.12 MHz. Find the wavelength in air and the period of the wave. Wavelength λ = c ÷ f = (3×10⁸ m/s) ÷ (27.12×10⁶ Hz) = 11.06 m. Period T = 1 ÷ f = 1 ÷ (27.12×10⁶) = 36.9 ns. The 11 m wavelength is far bigger than the body, so the field passes through tissue rather than being blocked by it.
chapters.trap: Thinking higher frequency penetrates deeper — it is the opposite, penetration falls as frequency rises. Also, 27.12 MHz is a reserved industrial frequency, not any random short-wave radio band, and diathermy heating is not surgical cautery.
chapters.prereq: Basic AC circuits: frequency, wavelength, impedance.
chapters.leave: Electrosurgical safety, macro- and micro-shock and leakage current go to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: A controlled current pulse through skin can excite a nerve or a muscle, and that is used to relieve pain, retrain muscle, or find a nerve during surgery.
chapters.depth: TENS for pain (gate-control theory), EMS/NMES for muscle re-education, FES for paralysed muscle, interferential therapy, Russian current (2.5 kHz bursts), galvanic (DC) and faradic (AC) currents. Pulse parameters: amplitude 0–100 mA, width 50–400 µs, frequency 1–150 Hz, charge per pulse, duty cycle. Muscle and nerve stimulators: a hand-held probe used to locate a motor nerve during surgery, and surface stimulators. Nerve conduction velocity measurement itself stays in Unit 1.

figure.aria: Block diagram of a nerve stimulator: battery, oscillator, pulse shaper, constant-current output stage and skin electrodes.

chapters.example: A TENS unit is set to 20 mA, pulse width 200 µs and frequency 100 Hz. Find the charge in one pulse, the charge delivered per second, and the duty cycle. Charge per pulse = I × t = 20×10⁻³ A × 200×10⁻⁶ s = 4 µC. Pulses per second = 100, so charge per second = 4 µC × 100 = 400 µC/s = 0.4 mC/s. Duty cycle = (200 µs × 100) ÷ 1 s = 0.02 = 2 %. The nerve sees a short high-current pulse, but the average current is only about 0.4 mA.
chapters.trap: Confusing pulse frequency with the internal carrier, and assuming more current is always better — charge density at the electrode decides whether the skin burns. TENS acts on sensory nerves for pain, EMS acts on motor nerves to make muscle contract.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: action potential, nerve conduction, EMG recording. Unit 6: current limits for safety.
chapters.leave: Nerve conduction velocity measurement goes to Unit 1; microshock and leakage current to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Lithotripsy breaks a kidney stone into small pieces with focused shock waves, so the pieces pass out in urine without open surgery.
chapters.depth: Extracorporeal shock-wave lithotripsy (ESWL): generation by spark gap (electrohydraulic), electromagnetic or piezoelectric source; focusing by an ellipsoid reflector with foci F1 and F2; coupling by water bath or gel pad; stone located by X-ray or ultrasound; 2000–3000 shocks per session at 60–120 shocks/min. Intracorporeal methods: laser and ultrasonic lithotripsy. Ancillary: ureteric stent, analgesia, hydration.

figure.aria: Block diagram of shock-wave lithotripsy: spark gap at one focus, ellipsoid reflector, focused wave, stone at the second focus and fragments leaving.

chapters.example: A lithotripter fires a 1 µF capacitor charged to 20 kV, 2500 times in one session. Find the energy per shock and the total energy delivered. Energy per shock E = ½CV² = 0.5 × 1×10⁻⁶ F × (20×10³ V)² = 0.5 × 1×10⁻⁶ × 4×10⁸ = 200 J. Total = 200 J × 2500 = 500,000 J = 500 kJ. Only a small part of each 200 J reaches the stone; the rest is lost in the water path.
chapters.trap: Calling the shock wave an electric shock — it is an acoustic pressure wave, and the patient gets no current. Not every stone is suitable for ESWL; hard or very large stones may need intracorporeal laser or ultrasonic fragmentation.
chapters.prereq: None beyond basic physics of waves and focusing.
chapters.leave: The X-ray machine used for stone location goes to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Cold below about −40 °C kills tissue, so a cryoprobe cooled by liquid nitrogen or expanding gas is used to destroy lesions, and the same cold stores cells for later use.
chapters.depth: Cryosurgery with liquid nitrogen (−196 °C), nitrous oxide or argon (Joule–Thomson cooling) probes; ice crystal formation, thaw, and cell death; the freeze–thaw–freeze cycle. Applications: skin lesions and warts, tumour cryoablation, cardiac cryoablation for atrial fibrillation. Cryopreservation and storage in dewars for blood, semen and tissue. Safety: frostbite, asphyxiation, oxygen deficiency in closed rooms, venting of boil-off gas.

figure.aria: Block diagram of cryosurgery: liquid nitrogen cooling a probe, an ice front spreading, cell destruction and a thaw cycle.

chapters.example: Find the heat removed to freeze 1 g of tissue from 37 °C down to −20 °C. The tissue is 80 % water. Take specific heat of tissue as 3.5 kJ/kg·K and latent heat of fusion of water as 334 kJ/kg. Sensible heat = mcΔT = 0.001 kg × 3500 J/kg·K × 57 K = 199.5 J. Latent heat = 0.0008 kg × 334,000 J/kg = 267 J. Total ≈ 467 J for one gram. Liquid nitrogen takes about 199 kJ/kg to evaporate, so at least 2.3 g of nitrogen is needed if none of the cold is wasted.
chapters.trap: Mixing up cryotherapy (removing heat) with diathermy (adding heat), and believing −196 °C kills instantly — the ice front must reach the whole lesion and the thaw matters as much as the freeze.
chapters.prereq: Basic heat transfer: sensible heat, latent heat, specific heat.
chapters.leave: Cardiac cryoablation as an alternative to RF ablation is compared in 5.9.

chapters.idea: The protection circuit stops a defibrillator shock from destroying the ECG amplifier, and the ablation catheter delivers RF energy to burn the small patch of heart muscle that causes an arrhythmia.
chapters.depth: Protection circuit: series resistors at each electrode, a neon lamp or spark gap that breaks down at a few hundred volts, and clamp diodes at the amplifier input; recovery time after the shock; why defibrillator-proof leads are needed. Cardiac ablation: steerable catheter with a 4 mm tip electrode, mapping of the arrhythmia, RF generator at about 500 kHz, 20–50 W, tip temperature 60–70 °C, lesion a few millimetres deep; cryoablation as an alternative; complications such as perforation and tamponade.

figure.aria: Block diagram showing a defibrillator shock arriving at the ECG electrodes and being absorbed by the protection network before the ECG amplifier.

chapters.example: An RF ablation generator delivers 50 W into heart tissue that looks like 100 Ω. Find the current and the voltage at the tip. Current I = √(P ÷ R) = √(50 ÷ 100) = √0.5 = 0.707 A. Voltage V = √(P × R) = √(50 × 100) = √5000 = 70.7 V. Check: I × V = 0.707 × 70.7 = 50 W. That 70 V at 500 kHz is what the protection circuit must also survive if the patient is being monitored at the same time.
chapters.trap: Saying the protection circuit protects the patient — it protects the amplifier; the patient is protected by the paddles being applied away from the electrodes. Also, the neon lamp is not just an indicator lamp in this circuit, it is the shunt that fires over at high voltage.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: bio-amplifiers and the ECG recording system. 5.1 for the defibrillator. Unit 6 for electrical safety.
chapters.leave: ECG amplifier design and artefact removal go to Unit 1; leakage current and macro/micro-shock to Unit 6.
